5.0.0.en: 1 Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand. 2 Belshazzar, whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein. 3 Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them. 4 They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone.

5.0.1.en: "Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand" [1].

5.0.2.en: Some translate "shazzar" as "fire," while the word "Belshazzar (Bel-shar-usur) Bel-Sharra-Utsur" means "Bel protects the king."

5.0.3.en: Great feasts were a feature of ancient times. It is clear that the word "thousand" means vastness, and it represents an approximate number. It was the custom at Eastern banquets that the king or the head of the table sat on a raised platform, so that all those present could see him. Hence the expression "drank wine before the thousand" reveals the precision of the account and the description.

5.0.4.en: "Belshazzar, whiles he tasted the wine, commanded to bring the golden and silver vessels which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem; that the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, might drink therein.

5.1.0.en: Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them" [2-3].

5.1.1.en: The word "father" carries many meanings; here it means his grandfather or one of his ancestors.

5.1.2.en: While the Babylonian state was in danger from Persia, with Cyrus besieging the city, Belshazzar was occupied with holding a feast that gathered a thousand nobles who had come from every place, together with his wives and concubines. He thought it impossible for Cyrus or anyone else to storm the massive walls of the city, so he left Cyrus to besiege it, in contempt of him and of his army. The walls of Babylon, as Herodotus relates, were no less than 87 feet wide and 350 feet high, with 250 towers rising another 100 feet into the air. Therefore Belshazzar thought that Babylon could not be conquered.

5.1.3.en: The effort Belshazzar put into holding the feast, and the resources that were provided, cannot be estimated. All this was joined with his defiance of God. Instead of fasting in the time of the siege, and crying to God to rescue him and his city, he held a feast and used the sacred vessels for drinking, in an atmosphere of corruption and licentiousness, which reveals the king's persistence in an unfitting life.

5.1.4.en: Cyrus learned of the feast because of its vastness and because many were invited to take part in it, so he realized that the king and his men were drowned in wine, unconcerned with the affairs of their country, and he found it a golden opportunity to storm the city.

5.1.5.en: While Belshazzar was opening the feast, Cyrus' army was at the gates of Babylon. The pagan historian Xenophon tells us that Belshazzar's two commanders, Gobryas (Godatas, Gobryas), who had defected, betrayed him. One of them had been made a eunuch in order to disgrace him, and the other's son had been killed during his father's lifetime, for nothing except that he was hunting with him and his arrow struck before his, so he wanted to take revenge on him. Cyrus diverted many channels of the Euphrates and stormed the city suddenly.

5.1.6.en: The vessels were not brought for the enjoyment of the pleasure of drinking, but to insult God, to defile the vessels consecrated to the service of His temple, and to disgrace. To carry the insult further, they glorified the idols while drinking from them.

5.1.7.en: St. John Cassian, in the preface to his book "The Conferences," sees in this feast a warning to believers against being occupied with the sacred vessels of gold or silver, which wicked kings can plunder, and that they should rather care for the spiritual vessels, that is, the holy souls of believers, which cannot be seized.

5.1.8.en: * When you plan to build a true and moderate temple for God, not of lifeless stones but of the assembly of the saints, not a temporary building that dissolves but an eternal building that is not shaken, and you also want to sanctify to the Lord the most valuable vessels, not of dumb metals, of gold and silver, which the king of Babylon could take afterward and consecrate to the pleasures of his concubines and his nobles, but you fashion holy souls that shine with the uprightness of purity, righteousness, and cleanness, and bear Christ dwelling in them as King. Since you long to establish in a province (your inner self) the institutes of the East, especially Egypt, they arise in you without monasteries existing, although you yourself are perfect in all virtues and knowledge and are filled with all spiritual wealth.

5.1.9.en: St. John Cassian: the critics found their opportunity to attack the book through this chapter, for the two pagan historians of Babylon, Berosus and Abydenus, had already asserted that Nabonidus was the last king of Babylon, and that he held an honored position even after the Persians took Babylon. Yet this chapter says that Belshazzar was the last king of Babylon, and that he met death by being killed.

5.1.10.en: Archaeology has confirmed that everything the two historians mentioned, and also Daniel, is true. For it is stated in the Assyrian inscriptions that Sir Herbert Rawlinson found in 1854 that Belshazzar was the son of King Nabonidus and that he shared the rule with him, as we saw before in the introduction to the book (Daniel and archaeology). This agrees with the statement that Daniel was the third in the kingdom.

5.1.11.en: In the excavations at Ur an inscription of Nabonidus was found containing a prayer for himself and then for his firstborn son Bel-Shar-Usur. Such a prayer was offered only for those who held the rule. Documents of "cuneiform" writing were also found, which are characters used in Babylon, recording how Belshazzar offered sheep and calves in the temples of Sippar as sacrifices for the king.

5.1.12.en: Not long ago heavy floods struck a district of ancient Babylon called Hillah, and huge earthen jars appeared, filled with tablets representing receipts and contracts of a banking establishment in Babylon, from which it appears that Belshazzar had a house, secretaries, and guards.

5.1.13.en: This Belshazzar is perhaps the same as Belteshazzar mentioned in the Babylonian records, who carried out the duty of first deputy of the king. According to the Babylonian records he became king as deputy for his father in the year 553 B.C. and continued in this position until 539 B.C. Although Nabonidus was absent the whole time in Tema in the north of the Arabian Peninsula, he did not leave the kingship until Cyrus conquered Babylon.

5.1.14.en: As for why Belshazzar was left as king in Babylon, this goes back to the character of his father Nabonidus, who was a man with religious and cultural interests, and was also an archaeologist; he used to search the inscriptions of the ancient kings and the foundations and stones of public buildings, and search for documents that reveal the past. His religious interests were very strong, and his daughter was consecrated to the moon god, and it appears that his mother was a priestess of the temple of "Sin (Sun)," the moon god. This is what occupied him from the affairs of government, and it is clear to us, from what Assyriology has uncovered, that he spent most of the days of his reign not in Babylon but in Tema, and thus he left his son Belshazzar to rule Babylon, in the same way that Nebuchadnezzar did with his father Nabopolassar. These facts were presented to us by Raymond P. Dougherty, professor of Assyriology [New Haven, Yale 1929].

5.2.0.en: "They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone" [4].

5.2.1.en: Having defiled the sacred vessels, they praised the pagan gods as the givers of victory over the true God, as it is said in the book of Habakkuk: "Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous" (Hab 1:16). They ate and drank and were satisfied and grew fat, and they mocked God, the Giver of gifts.

5.2.2.en: The king brought the sacred vessels deliberately before drinking, and drunkenness kindled his corrupt feelings all the more, and drove him to persist in mockery. Moreover the king did not sin alone, but drove his nobles, his wives, and his concubines to share with him, so the feast turned into a council of scoffers.

5.2.3.en: * How great was their folly! While they drank from vessels of gold, they praised gods of wood and stone.

5.2.4.en: St. Jerome. St. Jerome sees that the gods of gold refer to those who attack the truth using rational arguments that seem acceptable, and the gods of silver refer to those who use rhetoric and oratory for the same purpose, while the gods of brass and iron refer to those who use poetry with its feeble nonsense, some of which has good taste and some of which carries folly. The gods of wood and stone refer to those who present obvious absurdities.

5.3.0.en: 5 In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote. 6 Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another. 7 The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers. And the king spake, and said to the wise men of Babylon, Whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom. 8 Then came in all the king's wise men: but they could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the interpretation thereof. 9 Then was king Belshazzar greatly troubled, and his countenance was changed in him, and his lords were astonied.

5.3.1.en: "In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick (the lampstand) upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote" [5].

5.3.2.en: St. Jerome comments on the expression "in the same hour" saying that the hand appeared in the same hour so that God might declare that what was happening was discipline because of his blasphemy and not for any other reason.

5.3.3.en: It is clear that the banquet was at night, since lampstands were present, and that it continued until midnight, when Cyrus took Babylon.

5.3.4.en: The hand appeared to the king without the nobles, so he was greatly confused and terrified, and the nobles were terrified with him, without having seen anything.

5.3.5.en: St. Jerome says that the writing came on the wall of the royal palace so that the king might realize that what was written concerned him personally.

5.4.0.en: "Then the king's countenance was changed, and his thoughts troubled him, so that the joints of his loins were loosed, and his knees smote one against another" [6].

5.4.1.en: A few moments earlier the king had thought himself a mighty god, mocking the true God and defiling His sanctuary, praising idols. Now he takes the position of the humble accused, and realizes that God is the true Judge. The king's bodily strength was loosed, his mind was confused, and he lost his composure and dignity among those invited to the feast. He was in a position not to be envied.

5.4.2.en: "The king cried aloud to bring in the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers."

5.4.3.en: "And the king spake, and said to the wise men of Babylon,

5.5.0.en: Whosoever shall read this writing, and shew me the interpretation thereof, shall be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about his neck, and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom" [7].

5.5.1.en: The king felt that the wounds of his mind were grave, so he summoned the magicians, the wise men, and the astrologers, perhaps he might find a remedy for his depths, but he felt that there was no healing for his wounds, and that he would not escape from the hands of the Almighty. He forgot that he was a king holding a feast for the nobles, so he sent to summon these men in great haste, to enter to him while he was still at the feast. He cried aloud, which is unbecoming for one who has authority! He had completely lost his nerves!

5.6.0.en: 1. Perhaps because he had grown old and been retired. 2. The honor that Daniel received from Nebuchadnezzar stirred up, over time, the hatred of the Babylonian wise men, for they felt that a man of foreign race and a captive had surpassed them all, so they made every effort after the death of Nebuchadnezzar to exclude him from the palace, so that the men of the palace would forget him completely, and this found agreeableness in the heart of the prophet Daniel, who did not want to be counted among the Magi and to be their chief. At the same time they distorted the image of the Jewish people and their worship in the eyes of the king. This appears clearly from what the king did when he held the feast and wanted to defile the divine sanctuaries while glorifying his idols. Thus they were able to remove every trace of Daniel from the royal palace. 3. With all that had come upon him, the king did not examine himself and review his conduct. He had defiled God's sanctuaries and glorified his idols, so it was fitting for him to seek the man of God and ask counsel from him to atone for what he had done, but instead of seeking the man of God he asked for the men of the idols, magicians and astrologers. God had terrified him, so it was fitting for him to seek one who could bring him the divine voice, but even in the midst of his confusion he sought the voice of his idols. He realized that he could not escape God's judgment, so he asked to find his comfort in the magicians. We can say that Belshazzar was blind, having closed his eyes to beholding the divine light.

5.6.1.en: By announcing the gifts he would give to whoever interpreted the vision for him, he made clear that his heart did not enjoy the fear of God. He had become almost dead, and yet in his hidden pride he thinks that he will enrich the one who interprets the vision for him, instead of promising repentance.

5.6.2.en: "Then came in all the king's wise men: but they could not read the writing, nor make known to the king the interpretation thereof.

5.7.0.en: Then was king Belshazzar greatly troubled, and his countenance was changed in him, and his lords were astonied" [8-9].

5.7.1.en: The writing appeared to them like a sealed book, as in (Isa 29:11), which they could not open and read. Or say that they became blind, unable to see. A veil was placed over their hearts, so they could not read.

5.7.2.en: God granted King Belshazzar to see the hidden hand writing on the wall, but He did not grant him the ability to read what was written. The wise men came to read, but they were like the blind. God allowed this so that the king's terror might increase, and everyone around him be terrified. Perhaps this event among a thousand nobles, besides the wives and concubines, caused the news of the vision to spread quickly, not only throughout the city but beyond it; which gave Cyrus reassurance and confidence that what he was doing must be accomplished quickly, because God's hand was supporting it. These events, which certainly reached Cyrus afterward in precise detail, moved him toward honoring Daniel and his people and his God, so he allowed the people to return to Jerusalem.

5.7.3.en: God condemned the wicked conduct of the king in that very hour, so the writing came not in a dream but as a tangible reality. The king realized that a punishment awaited him, therefore he was very afraid before knowing the interpretation. This shows that what the king had done was not out of ignorance but out of awareness and consciousness.

5.7.4.en: * Belshazzar saw the finger of a hand writing on the wall, and immediately the image of a material thing was impressed on his spirit through bodily senses, and when the vision ended the image remained in his thoughts, remaining visible in the spirit but not understood...

5.7.5.en: When he failed to discover the meaning, Daniel came immediately, and since his mind was enlightened by the Spirit of prophecy, he disclosed to the troubled king the prophetic meaning of the sign.

5.8.s.en: 3. Daniel is brought before the king:

5.8.0.en: 10 Now the queen, by reason of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banquet house: and the queen spake and said, O king, live for ever: let not thy thoughts trouble thee, nor let thy countenance be changed: 11 There is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; whom the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father, the king, I say, thy father, made master of the magicians, astrologers, Chaldeans, and soothsayers; 12 Forasmuch as an excellent spirit, and knowledge, and understanding, interpreting of dreams, and shewing of hard sentences, and dissolving of doubts, were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar: now let Daniel be called, and he will shew the interpretation. 13 Then was Daniel brought in before the king. And the king spake and said unto Daniel, Art thou that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Jewry? 14 I have even heard of thee, that the spirit of the gods is in thee, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom is found in thee. 15 And now the wise men, the astrologers, have been brought in before me, that they should read this writing, and make known unto me the interpretation thereof: but they could not shew the interpretation of the thing: 16 And I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations, and dissolve doubts: now if thou canst read the writing, and make known to me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about thy neck, and shalt be the third ruler in the kingdom.

5.8.1.en: "Now the queen, by reason of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banquet house: and the queen spake and said, O king, live for ever:

5.8.2.en: let not thy thoughts trouble thee, nor let thy countenance be changed:

5.8.3.en: There is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; whom the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father made master of the magicians, astrologers, Chaldeans, and soothsayers" [10-11].

5.8.4.en: It is clear that the queen had lived in the days of Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar's grandfather; she was most probably his wife, that is, Belshazzar's grandmother, and not his wife, because the latter was with the king at the feast. As for the grandmother, in wisdom and dignity she did not take part in the feast, for the presence of women with men at banquets was contrary to Eastern customs at that time. Yet the queen's way of addressing the king bears witness to the accuracy of the book, for in Babylon the queen mother had a high position in the royal house.

5.8.5.en: She reminded the king of Daniel, who was most likely retired or excluded, but we cannot be certain that Belshazzar had not heard of him, for many looked on him as an angel come down from heaven. The king was drowned in his pleasures, which made him ignore the man of God or not be concerned with him, and resist God Himself.

5.8.6.en: The queen rebuked him in a calm spirit, as though she were saying to him: "Why do you walk in darkness when God has given you a man who carries the torch of surpassing light?!"

5.8.7.en: "Forasmuch as an excellent spirit, and knowledge, and understanding, interpreting of dreams, and shewing of hard sentences, and dissolving of doubts, were found in the same Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar:

5.9.0.en: now let Daniel be called, and he will shew the interpretation" [12].

5.9.1.en: The aged queen distinguished between Daniel and the magicians. The magicians boasted that they were able to interpret dreams, but their boasting was false and vain, whereas Daniel enjoyed three divine gifts by which he surpassed everyone and was distinguished from them.

5.9.2.en: · In him is an excellent spirit.

5.9.3.en: · In him are knowledge and wisdom.

5.9.4.en: · He is able to interpret dreams, to show hard sentences, and to solve problems.

5.9.5.en: She also revealed Nebuchadnezzar's esteem for him, for he attributed him to his god, and gave him an honored name, "Belteshazzar." He bore a name similar to the name of the king, "Belshazzar." Therefore it was fitting for him not to despise him because he was of a foreign race and a captive!

5.9.6.en: "Then was Daniel brought in before the king. And the king spake and said unto Daniel,

5.9.7.en: Art thou that Daniel, which art of the children of the captivity of Judah, whom the king my father brought out of Jewry?

5.9.8.en: I have even heard of thee, that the spirit of the gods is in thee, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom is found in thee.

5.9.9.en: And now the wise men, the astrologers, have been brought in before me, that they should read this writing, and make known unto me the interpretation thereof: but they could not shew the interpretation of the thing:

5.9.10.en: And I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations, and dissolve doubts:

5.10.0.en: now if thou canst read the writing, and make known to me the interpretation thereof, thou shalt be clothed with scarlet, and have a chain of gold about thy neck, and shalt be the third ruler in the kingdom" [13-16].

5.10.1.en: With all that had come upon the king, and what he had heard from his grandmother, he did not humble himself, repenting of what he had done, but spoke with Daniel arrogantly, looking on him as a humble captive man. Perhaps he used this manner in order to bind him to obedience and to the commitment to speak the truth to him.

5.10.2.en: The king confessed that he had resorted to the magicians and their utter inability had appeared, and that he hoped, because of what he had heard about Daniel, that he would provide him with what these men were unable to.

5.10.3.en: The king made promises to Daniel of royal garments (purple), a golden chain, and authority, not knowing that he himself would lose his possessions, his authority, and even his life after a few hours. He was terrified before the divine judgment, and perhaps he felt that he was quickly losing everything, but he hid all this, making promises to others that he himself could not enjoy.

5.11.0.en: 17 Then Daniel answered and said before the king, Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another; yet I will read the writing unto the king, and make known to him the interpretation. 18 O thou king, the most high God gave Nebuchadnezzar thy father a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour: 19 And for the majesty that he gave him, all people, nations, and languages, trembled and feared before him: whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he set up; and whom he would he put down. 20 But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him: 21 And he was driven from the sons of men; and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven; till he knew that the most high God ruled in the kingdom of men, and that he appointeth over it whomsoever he will. 22 And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this; 23 But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know: and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified: 24 Then was the part of the hand sent from him; and this writing was written. 25 And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN. 26 This is the interpretation of the thing: MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. 27 TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. 28 PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. 29 Then commanded Belshazzar, and they clothed Daniel with scarlet, and put a chain of gold about his neck, and made a proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.

5.11.1.en: "Then Daniel answered and said before the king,

5.11.2.en: Let thy gifts be to thyself, and give thy rewards to another;

5.11.3.en: yet I will read the writing unto the king, and make known to him the interpretation" [17].

5.11.4.en: Daniel showed his disdain for temporal gifts before reading the writing and interpreting it, lest the king think that the refusal was not from the depths of the heart, but because Daniel realized that his kingdom was ending, as though Daniel were exploiting the vision for his personal benefit. In any case, as St. Jerome says: [Daniel followed the evangelical commandment, refusing any reward, for it is said: "freely ye have received, freely give"]. His heart was not bound to wealth or honor or authority, and on the other hand he realized that it was not in Belshazzar's power to give these things, because the hour of his destruction had come.

5.11.5.en: Daniel's manner of interpreting the vision here differed from that with Nebuchadnezzar. He showed his disregard for the reward, for the following reasons.

5.11.6.en: · The king's sin here is not out of ignorance, for he already knew what happened with his grandfather.

5.11.8.en: · Belshazzar glorified the idols and praised them with the intention of insulting the living God.

5.11.9.en: The writing came: "Numbered, numbered, weighed, divisions," and its meaning: God has numbered your kingdom, or assessed it, and finished it. You were weighed in the balances and found wanting. Your kingdom is divided and given to the empire of the Medes and Persians.

5.11.10.en: St. Jerome says: [By this the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah concerning the collapse of the kingdom of Babylon during the holding of the feast was fulfilled in a precise, literal way, for he says: "My heart panted, fearfulness affrighted me: the night of my pleasure hath he turned into fear unto me. Prepare the table, watch in the watchtower, eat, drink: arise, ye princes, and anoint the shield" (Isa 21:4-5)].

5.11.11.en: "O thou king, the most high God gave Nebuchadnezzar thy father a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour:

5.11.12.en: And for the majesty that he gave him, all people, nations, and languages, trembled and feared before him:

5.11.13.en: whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he set up; and whom he would he put down.

5.12.0.en: But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him" [18-20].

5.12.1.en: Daniel made clear to him that what his grandfather King Nebuchadnezzar enjoyed was nothing but a divine gift, for all authority is from God (Rom 8:1), since God wishes His power to appear in a visible way through kingdoms. But he misused the gift, and instead of glorifying God and serving people his heart became proud and arrogant.

5.12.2.en: Nebuchadnezzar was a man of authority who killed whom he would and spared whom he would; raised whom he would and humbled whom he would, and he did not realize that the lives of people are in the hand of God, and even the king's own life, honor, and authority, all of these are in the hand of God.

5.12.3.en: * If this is the case (the king can do what he wishes), the question arises: how are we to understand what is said in the Holy Bible, "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will" (Prov 21:1). Perhaps we can say that every saint is a king, because sin does not reign in his mortal body, and so his heart remains kept in safety, because it is in the hand of God (Rom 6). Once he is placed in the hand of God the Father, according to the Gospel, no one is able to snatch him away. As for one who is snatched away, it is understood that he was never in the hand of God.

5.13.0.en: St. Jerome "And he was driven from the sons of men; and his heart was made like the beasts, and his dwelling was with the wild asses: they fed him with grass like oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven; till he knew that the most high God ruled in the kingdom of men, and that he appointeth over it whomsoever he will" [21].

5.13.1.en: What happened with Nebuchadnezzar is a grave matter, reckoned a lesson for successive generations, yet behold his grandson Belshazzar quickly forgot the lesson or pretended to forget it, and did not benefit from the experience of his grandfather, who because of his arrogance withdrew from humanity to live in the kingdom of the dumb beasts like one without reason. This is what his grandson did of his own will when he held the feast without reason and defiled the divine sanctuaries, thinking that he was making light of God.

5.14.0.en: "And thou his son, O Belshazzar, hast not humbled thine heart, though thou knewest all this" [22].

5.14.1.en: He calls Belshazzar a son of King Nebuchadnezzar, who fell under divine discipline because of his pride; as though he were saying to him: "I am not presenting to you an example from a foreign nation, but from the house of your father and your family. You are without excuse!"

5.14.2.en: St. Jerome says: [Some see that the speech here applies to the Antichrist, for just as Belshazzar did not benefit from the discipline of his father Nebuchadnezzar who fell into pride, so the Antichrist does not benefit from what befell his father the devil because of his pride. And just as the kingdom passed from Belshazzar after he was killed to another, so the Antichrist dies and the saints reign instead of him.

5.14.3.en: "But hast lifted up thyself against the Lord of heaven; and they have brought the vessels of his house before thee, and thou, and thy lords, thy wives, and thy concubines, have drunk wine in them; and thou hast praised the gods of silver, and gold, of brass, iron, wood, and stone, which see not, nor hear, nor know:

5.14.4.en: and the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified:

5.14.5.en: Then was the part of the hand sent from him; and this writing was written.

5.14.6.en: And this is the writing that was written,

5.14.8.en: This is the interpretation of the thing:

5.14.9.en: MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it.

5.14.10.en: TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.

5.14.11.en: PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.

5.15.0.en: Then commanded Belshazzar, and they clothed Daniel with scarlet, and put a chain of gold about his neck, and made a proclamation concerning him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom" [29].

5.15.1.en: The king gave him his gifts, but they lasted only for hours. Perhaps the prophet Daniel accepted them lest the king think that he was rebelling against him or acting insolently and proudly toward him. Daniel put on a royal purple robe and a chain of gold, which points to royal authority... Thus an opportunity was given to Cyrus to get to know him and ask the reason for his honor, and so hear of the vision.

5.15.2.en: St. Jerome explains the king's offering of the reward to Daniel by saying that he thought this painful prophecy would be fulfilled in the distant future, or that by honoring the man of God he would find mercy and grace with God.

5.16.0.en: 30 In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. 31 And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old. [30-31].

5.16.1.en: While the drinking from the cups of the house of the Lord was going on, before morning, Cyrus entered Babylon in a way the guards and watchmen in the high towers did not expect, for the river Euphrates overflowed beneath the massive walls of Babylon. The Persians had dug a huge channel outside Babylon without the Babylonians knowing of it. Quickly they connected the channel to the river, so the water flowed into the channel, and the army crossed into the city through the dry riverbed under the walls. From inside the city they opened the gates, and the soldiers stormed the city from every side, and Belshazzar was killed that same night or perhaps the following night. The kingdom was transferred from the hands of the Babylonians to the Persians; thus we pass from the golden head of the statue to the chest and shoulders of silver, as is stated in the second chapter of the book.

5.16.2.en: The pagan historians speak with astonishment of Cyrus' occupation of Babylon, for the two commanders who defected from Belshazzar revealed to him the way to conquer the city.

5.17.0.en: The word Darius in Persian means "possessor of good," and it is a title of the Persian kings like Pharaoh for Egypt and Caesar for Rome.

5.17.1.en: Some see that Darius the Mede is the same as Cyaxares II, son of Astyages, the maternal uncle of Cyrus, who gave him the throne of Babylon as a partner in the rule. And as Fr. Abdel Messih Basit Abu El-Kheir says, it is stated in the book that "Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" (Dan 9:1). "Was made king" here means "was made ruler" over Babylon, that is, he was a partner ruler and deputy for King Cyrus. The book also says that the kingdom was not given to the Mede alone, but "to the Medes and Persians" (Dan 5:28), and the king ruled by one common law, "the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not" (Dan 6:8, 15), which Darius could not change or contradict; that is, the prophet Daniel speaks of one united empire, the empire of the Medes and Persians, and does not speak of two successive empires. Nor was it possible for him to amend or change or resist the law of "the Medes and Persians," the law of the united kingdom. Daniel did not speak of the war that arose between the Babylonians and the Medes; Isaiah spoke of it (Isa 50-51). We have no need to point out the alliance between the Medes and the Persians, especially in their occupation of Babylon under the leadership of Darius and Cyrus, where the two occupied the city.

5.17.2.en: St. Jerome says: [After he (Belshazzar) was killed by Darius king of the Medes, the maternal uncle of Cyrus the Persian, the empire of the Chaldeans was shattered by Cyrus the Persian. Isaiah spoke in chapter 21 of the two kingdoms (the Medes and the Persians) as the drivers of a chariot drawn by a camel and an ass (Isa 21:7)].

5.17.3.en: Some see that he is Gubaru, or Gubarn, or Gobryas, the commander-in-chief of Cyrus, who occupied Babylon and had an effective role. It is stated in the cuneiform inscriptions, discovered and published in the twentieth century, that Cyrus appointed his army commander Gubaru governor over Babylon as soon as he conquered it, and he in turn appointed governors in Babylon. This means that Cyrus handed him the leadership of the country and the appointment of governors, while he himself went out to achieve victory over the rest of the lands. The Cuneiform tablets also mentioned his name as governor of Babylon and Mesopotamia, that is, Babylon, Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine, for fourteen years, and his name struck terror into the hearts of criminals.

5.17.4.en: Others see that Cyrus himself was called Darius.

5.17.5.en: Herodotus did not refer to Darius as a king because of the weakness of his character and his corruption, especially since he handed the throne to his nephew (his sister's son) Cyrus. Darius was sixty-two years old, which agrees with what is stated in Xenophon that he was Cyaxares II.

5.18.s.en: Why did God allow Daniel to wear the purple?

5.18.0.en: The life of Daniel presents to us a living picture of God's dealings with us. From time to time God is glorified in the life of Daniel and uses him to serve His captive people. But as much as God was glorified in him, the enemy of good was planning to destroy him, and the plan turned into the building up of the Kingdom of God. Now that Daniel appeared to be off the stage, God draws him to the palace through Belshazzar's vision, and it ends with his wearing the purple and the chain of gold on his neck and becoming the third man in the kingdom. This did not last more than a few hours, for Cyrus took Babylon and killed King Belshazzar, and found Daniel in this garment, and when he asked about him he learned that he had prophesied the fall of the kingdom of Babylon and the rise of the kingdom of Persia, and the victory of Cyrus, etc. He honored him and drew him near as a man of God, and sympathized with his people. It is as though God allowed what is recorded in this chapter at the decisive moments of the fall of Babylon and the victory of Persia so that Cyrus would listen to Daniel and his people, and hear the prophecies of the prophet Jeremiah about their return after seventy years of captivity, and so he issued his decree to that effect (Ezra 1:1-4).

5.18.1.en: Let me enjoy the banquet of Your love,
